transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will not participate in the High Court's first case
to be argued in the new term next week.
The case is a major test of when and if state and local governments can sue fossil fuel
companies for allegedly deceiving the public about environmental harms that companies knew
existed.
Here's NPR's Nina Totenberg.
Alito has long held financial interests in energy companies, but did not recuse himself
last February when the Supreme Court agreed to hear a major climate change case.
Now, however, one week before arguments in the case are to take place, the Court indicated
that Alito will not participate.
While he gave no reason, it appears that he owns stock in two companies facing similar
lawsuits that have been paused while the Supreme Court ponders the issue.
Alito's decision could lead to a four-to-four tie at the High Court, but most climate change
experts see that as unlikely given that the case is viewed as a longshot.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
Residents of Seabright, New Jersey cleaning up after that nora-easter that hit the east
coast over the weekend, forcing airlines to cancel hundreds of flights, knocking out power
to tens of thousands of homes and businesses, and flooding low-lying areas in New Jersey
and New York City.
Mike Riley was out Monday trying to put his property to rights.
When you live down here, we're kind of ready for it, it kind of happens all the time.
You can get the lightest little rain, you're going to have flooding, but this nora-easter
was a little bit more than just flooding, so we had probably around three feet of water
over here.
And the Pacific forecasters say Hurricane Polo is nearing landfall on Mexico's Baja California
Peninsula.
Polo is a Category 3 storm in the National Hurricane Center in Miami as warning of life-threatening
winds and flash flooding.
Pope Leo urged Europe to seek peace as he wrapped up a four-day trip to France and Piers
Eleanor Beardsley reports.
Pope Leo spoke in the city of Mess in the Alsace-Lorraine region long disputed by France
and Germany.
"Today, unfortunately, war has come again to Europe," he said, "where pointless massacres
are taking civilian lives."
Leo said Europe can stop the spiral of violence.
"You have demonstrated over the past 80 years of peace that it's possible to express divergent
opinions, demands, and interests through dialogue rather than confrontation," he said.
The Pope also called on Europe to welcome those fleeing persecution and wars.
That means integrating them as if into your own family, he said.
The Pope called the migrants' arrival in Europe an exceptional encounter between peoples and
cultures.
Eleanor Beardsley in Piers News, Paris.
"British police say the five men arrested near a U.S.-run air base in England will be
released on bail.
The U.K.'s head of counterterrorism policing says the men face stringent conditions and
remain under investigation.
Investigators looking into a possible link to Iran, Russia, or non-state-backed military
groups."
This is NPR.
The U.S. Navy says two Navy aviators are being evaluated by medical personnel after they
were forced to eject from their aircraft.
The Navy says the incident happened off the coast of Virginia during aircraft recovery
operations aboard the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower and that four Navy personnel on board the
ship were injured.
Over 30 artists contributed to a new anti-ICE compilation album out later this week, including
Fred Armisen and Tony Morello.
The benefit album is raising funds for immigrant rights organizations in California, and Piers'
Isabella Gomez Sarmiento reports.
"Contra Ice Volume 1" spans across music, comedy, and spoken word.
American activist Kathleen Hanna contributed a cover of the song "Let Me Love You" by
DJ Snake and Justin Bieber.
Hanna tells NPR that she is deeply upset by ICE raids in her community in Los Angeles.
She says she hopes Contra Ice will inspire listeners to take action and stand up for
what they believe in.
"I think it reminds people of all the different ways there are to protest."
ICE has so far not responded to NPR's request for comment on the creation and mission of
the album.
Isabella Gomez Sarmiento, NPR News.
The NFL wants the Homeland Security Department to take down a social media video featuring
highlights of violent hits by Hall of Fame player Brian Dawkins, in reference to a potential
caravan of immigrants approaching the U.S. border.
The video, as posted Sunday, remains up on the department's X account and a text to ESPN.
Dawkins said he had not given permission.
This is NPR News.

Residents of Seabright, New Jersey cleaning up after nor'easter caused flooding and power outages
Hurricane Polo nearing landfall on Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as Category 3 storm
Pope Leo urged Europe to seek peace during four-day trip to France
Five men arrested near U.S. air base in England released on bail under investigation
Two Navy aviators ejected from aircraft off Virginia coast during USS Dwight D. Eisenhower operations
Over 30 artists contributed to anti-ICE benefit compilation album for immigrant rights organizations
NFL requests Homeland Security remove Brian Dawkins video used in immigrant border caravan post
